title: Given a set of meetings with start and end times, find the minimum number of rooms needed so that no two overlapping meetings share a room.
shortTitle: Minimum Meeting Rooms Required (Interval Scheduling with a Heap)

s1_definition.oneliner: Sort meetings by start, use a min-heap of end times to free finished rooms before each meeting, and the peak heap size is the room count.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Peak concurrency** – the minimum number of rooms equals the maximum number of meetings active at any single instant.
- **Min-heap of end times** – tracks the end time of each occupied room; the soonest-ending meeting is at the root.
- **Free-then-occupy** – before seating a new meeting, poll any room whose end time is at or before the new start; then offer the new end.
- **Heap size = rooms** – the heap size at any moment is the number of concurrent meetings; its maximum is the answer.
- **Two-pointer alternative** – separate and sort all starts and ends, walk both pointers, increment on starts and decrement on ends.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh schedules customer advisory sessions throughout the day. He processes sessions in start-time order, keeping a tray of busy-until times. Before seating a new session he removes any room from the tray whose session has ended. Then he seats the new session. The largest the tray ever grows is the minimum number of rooms he needs.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
     Meeting Rooms: Heap Processing

     Meetings (sorted): [0,30], [5,10], [15,20]

     Step 1: Seat [0,30]
     Heap: [30]
     Rooms: 1

     Step 2: Seat [5,10]
     heap.peek()=30 > 5 => no room freed
     Heap: [10, 30]
     Rooms: 2  ← peak

     Step 3: Seat [15,20]
     heap.peek()=10 <= 15 => free room ending at 10
     Heap: [30]
     Offer 20: Heap: [20, 30]
     Rooms: 2

     Answer: 2 rooms

     Timeline view:
     0    5    10   15   20   25   30
     |============================| Room 1: [0,30]
          |====|                    Room 2: [5,10]
                    |====|          Room 2: [15,20] (reused)
     Peak overlap at t=5: 2 meetings active
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The minimum number of meeting rooms equals the maximum number of meetings that overlap at any single instant. This reframing from "scheduling" to "peak concurrency" is the key conceptual leap that makes the problem tractable.

The heap approach sorts meetings by start time and uses a min-heap of end times. Before seating each new meeting, poll any room whose end time is at or before the new start. Then offer the new meeting's end time. The heap size at any moment equals the concurrent meetings, and the maximum size is the answer. The two-pointer alternative separates and sorts starts and ends, then walks both, tracking a running room count.

The tie-handling decision matters: using less-than-or-equal allows back-to-back reuse (a room freed at 10 hosts a meeting starting at 10), while strict less-than requires a separate room. This is a domain choice, not a coding choice.

At National Bank of India, Rajesh uses this to provision advisory rooms across a day of customer bookings. The same model applies to connection pool sizing, CPU thread scheduling, and airport gate assignment: any resource allocation problem about peak simultaneous demand is this problem in disguise.

Remember one sentence: sort by start, use a min-heap of end times to free finished rooms, and the peak heap size is the minimum number of rooms.

---

keyPoints: Minimum rooms equals maximum overlap: the peak number of concurrent meetings at any instant.
Sort by start, then use a min-heap of end times: poll the root if it ends before the new start, then offer the new end.
The heap size at any moment is the number of concurrent meetings; its maximum is the answer.
The two-pointer sweep separates and sorts starts and ends, incrementing on starts and decrementing on ends.
Tie handling: <= allows back-to-back room reuse; < does not. This is a domain decision.
This pattern models CPU scheduling, connection pool sizing, airport gates, and any peak-demand resource allocation.
